digest.title: Material Intelligence
digest.description: An AI-generated weekly digest of AI developments in materials science.
digest.overview: This week: AI-assisted crystal structure determination, extraction of experimental diffraction data, and new ways to navigate and simulate materials. All studies covered are preprints, assessed from abstracts rather than full papers.

stories.title: AI-assisted search combines diffraction and energetics to resolve crystal structures
stories.summary: The XCAPE framework combines powder X-ray diffraction, composition, cell parameters and space group with an evolutionary search accelerated by a machine-learning interatomic potential. It recovered 71 of 77 structures from simulated patterns and all 12 reference structures tested with experimental patterns. Of 12 additional candidate assignments, 10 were within 10 meV per atom of the convex hull in density functional theory calculations.
stories.whyItMatters: Combining diffraction agreement with physical plausibility could narrow the space of possible structures when overlapping peaks make diffraction alone ambiguous.
stories.limitation: This is an abstract-only preprint. The additional assignments are candidates, not independently confirmed structures; the reported experimental-pattern benchmark contains 12 reference structures.

sources.title: Physics-Guided Crystal Structure Elucidation from Powder X-Ray Diffraction with Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
sources.evidence: Determining unique atomic coordinates from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) remains challenging because peak overlap, weak scattering from light elements, limited scattering contrast between elements with similar atomic numbers, and experimental noise render the inverse problem underdetermined. Here, we present XCAPE (XRD-Constrained Accelerated Prediction Engine), a crystal structure prediction (CSP) framework that integrates experimentally derived composition, unit cell parameters, space group, and PXRD data into a symmetry-aware evolutionary search. XCAPE explores Wyckoff-site configurations using tailored mutation operations, evaluates candidates by both energetic stability and diffraction agreement, and accelerates geometry optimization using a universal machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). The framework recovered 71 of 77 database-derived benchmark structures (92.2%) from simulated PXRD patterns and all 12 reference structures from experimental PXRD patterns. It further identified 12 candidate structure assignments that are consistent with experimental PXRD patterns, lack matching entries in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD), and are thermodynamically competitive at the MLIP level. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations showed that 10 of these 12 candidates lie within 10 meV/atom of the convex hull. By bridging experimental diffraction data and physically plausible atomistic models, XCAPE can provide structural insight into previously unresolved materials and support accelerated materials discovery in automated research workflows.

stories.title: Vision models recover diffraction curves from published figures
stories.summary: A pipeline uses a vision language model to locate diffraction plots and sketch curves, then classical computer vision to refine them. Applied to 3,954 covalent organic framework articles, it produced 11,445 calibrated curves in the open COF-PEAK database. Against hand digitization of 60 panels, the median peak-position difference was 0.07 degrees.
stories.whyItMatters: Recovering full curves from figures can make experimental evidence reusable for comparing framework structures and synthesis conditions, beyond the few peak positions often reported in text.
stories.limitation: This is an abstract-only preprint. The reported comparison covers 60 panels; peak-position accuracy alone does not establish that intensities and every extracted curve are reliable.

sources.title: Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
sources.evidence: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

stories.title: Fast AI navigation is tested on simulated microscopy images
stories.summary: Researchers compared vision-language-model decision methods for navigating simulated scanning transmission electron microscopy images of a tungsten dopant and a grain boundary in monolayer MoS2. A method that reads probabilities of candidate labels took 0.13–0.21 seconds per decision. Dopant navigation succeeded 66–91% of the time across the tested models; the best model achieved 43% success on the grain-boundary task.
stories.whyItMatters: Fast, language-directed decisions could help automate the search for local defects and interfaces during materials characterization.
stories.limitation: This is an abstract-only preprint using simulated images, not a demonstration on a live microscope. The grain-boundary success rate also leaves substantial room for improvement.

sources.title: Fast closed-loop STEM navigation using vision-language models with typed decisions
sources.evidence: Closed-loop scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), in which each acquired image determines the next field of view and magnification, offers a route to autonomous atomic-scale materials analysis. Such a loop would automate navigation to defects and grain boundaries, a task that has long relied on operator judgment, and would enable systematic analysis of diverse local structures at scale. Realizing it hinges on the decision step, which must translate each acquired image into the next operation both quickly and correctly; yet which decision method can deliver both remains unclear. Here, we isolate this decision step. Using simulated atomic-resolution STEM images of a substitutional W dopant and a grain boundary in monolayer MoS$_2$, where the true target position is known and every method starts from identical conditions, we compared four vision-language models (VLMs) and three decision methods. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of Typed Decision, which directly obtains the probabilities of candidate labels from a pretrained VLM, for closed-loop STEM navigation. Typed Decision showed the shortest decision latency for all models (0.13-0.21 s) and generally achieved the highest navigation success rate among the three methods: it was the best for all models in W dopant navigation (66-91%) and for the best-performing model, Cosmos-Reason2 32B, in grain boundary navigation (43%). Furthermore, navigation to the different targets, the W dopant and the grain boundary, was possible by natural-language specification alone, without task-specific training of the VLM. These results indicate that Typed Decision is an effective decision method for realizing fast, accurate, and flexible closed-loop STEM.

stories.title: Fatigue simulations expose a potential blind spot in foundation potentials
stories.summary: A preprint compares an embedded-atom method potential with the NequIP foundation potential under nanoscale fatigue loading. Although both agree with reference data for many near-equilibrium properties, NequIP predicts a stacking-fault energy roughly seven times lower than the other potential and substantially more plastic deformation during cycling.
stories.whyItMatters: Agreement on equilibrium benchmarks does not necessarily establish reliability for rare, externally driven events. Fatigue and fracture simulations may need validation targeted to the mechanisms being studied.
stories.limitation: The comparison does not establish which potential predicts fatigue correctly: the authors note that direct experimental validation is unavailable. The report is an abstract-only preprint.

sources.title: Emergent Fatigue Dynamics from Foundational Interatomic Potentials
sources.evidence: Foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials are trained on large, diverse DFT datasets, but their validation rests on equilibrium states, which does not guarantee correct emergent behavior in large-scale molecular dynamics. Where no direct experimental validation is available, comparisons to physically motivated potentials are valuable for drawing insight. We distinguish static properties, which are thermally accessible, from emergent properties, which require work from an external fatigue stress to drive rare events, and compare the potentials on both. An EAM potential and the NequIP foundational potential both agree closely with reference data for many near-equilibrium properties, but NequIP predicts an anomalously low intrinsic stacking fault energy ($\sim7$ times lower than EAM) and thus predicts far more plastic deformation under fatigue cycling of a nanoscale flaw modeled after the classical Griffith crack problem. Per-atom energy distributions after loading show that the two potentials differ most at energies far above what is thermally accessible. We also document memory-related crashes and silent extrapolation as practical concerns for practitioners of these foundational model forms.

stories.title: Diffusion model generates grain boundaries at target energies
stories.summary: A symmetry-constrained diffusion model generates paired, equivalent grain boundaries in periodic cells, making the energy of an individual boundary a well-defined target. For an aluminum boundary, all 350 generated structures retained equivalent boundary pairs after relaxation. For three in-range targets with ample nearby training examples, 44–70% fell within 0.1 J/m² of the target energy.
stories.whyItMatters: Conditioning generation on a boundary property could make interfaces a more direct design variable and help researchers explore potentially metastable structures.
stories.limitation: This is an abstract-only preprint for one aluminum grain-boundary geometry. Energies were supplied by a machine-learning potential, and target tracking weakened at high energies and failed outside the training range.

sources.title: Generating grain boundary structures at a specified energy with a symmetry-constrained diffusion model
sources.evidence: Grain boundaries (GBs) govern many properties of polycrystalline materials, and inverse design would make the GB structure itself a design variable. Crystal generative models such as MatterGen operate on periodic cells, which contain two GBs. The cell energy defines a single GB only when the two are equivalent, but existing models do not enforce this equivalence. Building on MatterGen, we developed a symmetry-constrained diffusion model in which the two GBs are related by a symmetry operation: atoms near one GB are generated, and those near the other are reconstructed through a symmetry projection applied at every denoising step. We applied it to the $Σ5(210)[001]$ symmetric tilt GB in Al, conditioning generation on the GB energy from a machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP). All 350 generated structures kept a geometrically equivalent GB pair after relaxation. Given a target GB energy, the model generated structures at that energy: for the three in-range targets with many nearby training structures, 44% to 70% fell within $\pm 0.1$ J/m$^2$ of the target. Tracking weakened at higher energies and failed outside the training range. Of the 91 near-target structures, 90 matched no training structure under the adopted geometric criterion, indicating that the model can propose configurations near the target energy that are distinct from the training structures, a capability that could help identify unknown metastable GB structures observed in experiments. Building GB-pair equivalence into generation thus makes GB properties well-defined design targets, enabling inverse design of GB structures.

stories.title: Calibration links predicted and measured thermal conductivity
stories.summary: Researchers combined a machine-learning model for calculated lattice thermal conductivity with a temperature-dependent correction derived from literature measurements of half-Heusler compounds. Calculations generally overestimated measured values; on chemistries withheld from fitting, the calibrated method predicted measurements about as closely as independent laboratories agreed with one another.
stories.whyItMatters: Explicitly addressing the gap between ideal-crystal calculations and polycrystalline measurements could make thermoelectric screening more useful for selecting experimental candidates.
stories.limitation: This is an abstract-only preprint restricted to cubic, 18-valence-electron half-Heuslers. The correction did not consistently improve every compound, and the data do not establish a single cause of the calculation–measurement gap.

sources.title: Prediction of lattice thermal conductivity of half-Heusler compounds by machine learning and transfer-function calibration
sources.evidence: High-throughput searches for half-Heusler thermoelectrics increasingly rely on lattice thermal conductivity ($κ_L$) from first-principles calculations, or from machine-learning models trained on them. These calculations describe an ideal single crystal, whereas measurements are made on polycrystalline samples, in which grain boundaries and defects scatter heat as well. The resulting gap between calculated and measured $κ_L$ has been noted for individual compounds but not, to our knowledge, quantified across a materials class, so the values used for screening carry an unknown, systematic bias. Here we quantify and correct this bias for cubic half-Heusler compounds with 18 valence electrons. Using a curated literature corpus that keeps calculated and measured values apart, we show that calculations overestimate measured $κ_L$ in most bonding families, and that the excess shrinks with temperature. Scattering by defects, added to the intrinsic scattering between lattice vibrations, would give such a trend, but the data do not single out one cause. A simple transfer function with this temperature dependence removes the median offset, and refitting its magnitude within a bonding family lowers the median error further, though not consistently compound by compound. Combined with a machine-learning model that predicts the calculated value from crystal structure, and tested on chemistries withheld from all fitting, the method predicts measured $κ_L$ in this class about as closely as independent laboratories agree with one another, and provides testable predictions for compounds not yet measured.

stories.title: Neural adsorption framework screens thousands of carbon-capture materials
stories.summary: A neural classical density functional framework calculated predicted adsorption isotherms for more than 5,000 experimentally reported metal-organic frameworks. The authors identify four isotherm shapes and use predicted working capacity and regeneration energy to assess suitability for different capture processes.
stories.whyItMatters: Screening across low and high loadings can reveal process-relevant differences that a low-pressure Henry constant alone cannot distinguish.
stories.limitation: This is an abstract-only preprint. The screening results are computational predictions, not evidence that the identified candidates achieve the projected capture performance in operation.

sources.title: Characterizing adsorption thermodynamics in carbon capture materials: an efficient first-principles approach
sources.evidence: Porous materials offer a vast design space for CO$_2$ capture, whose exploration hinges on efficient and accurate first-principles predictions of the thermodynamics governing adsorption. However, simulating isotherms and heats of adsorption using grand canonical molecular simulations is extremely computationally expensive when combined with accurate ab initio treatments of the molecular interactions, limiting screening to low-pressure uptake encoded in the Henry constant. Identifying and designing the best CO$_2$ capture materials requires a strategy that can efficiently calculate their adsorption properties using ab initio potential energy surfaces such as those now available from foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs). Here we develop a neural classical density functional (cDFT) framework for carbon capture processes that allows direct calculation of adsorption isotherms from low to high loading limits of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) without grand canonical simulations. We demonstrate the success of our approach by calculating the ab initio adsorption isotherms for over 5,000 experimentally reported MOFs. From our screening, we show how these materials can be characterized using four isotherm shapes, arising from their pore size and binding sites, which the Henry constant cannot distinguish. We show that these shapes, rather than the binding strength alone, decide which MOFs suit which process: small pores with strong binding sites for vacuum and temperature swings at low pressure, large pores with weakly binding walls for pressure swings. Finally, we identify the most promising candidates by weighing their working capacity against the energy needed for regeneration.

stories.title: Agent combines learned predictions with first-principles band workflows
stories.summary: Perfumer couples Quantum ESPRESSO with learned models for structural pre-relaxation and electronic band prediction. The authors report a 2.75-fold overall speedup from learned pre-relaxation followed by Quantum ESPRESSO refinement. Their band model achieved a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials from held-out composition families.
stories.whyItMatters: A natural-language interface and faster preliminary calculations could make relaxation-to-band workflows easier to run across many candidate materials.
stories.limitation: This is an abstract-only preprint. The speedup applies to the tested structures and includes first-principles refinement; predicted band energies remain approximate and should not be treated as experimental measurements.

sources.title: Perfumer: A Large Language Model-based Agentic Framework Accelerating Structural Relaxation and Electronic Band Prediction for First-Principle Calculation
sources.evidence: First-principles structural relaxation and band calculations require substantial computation and expertise. Here we present Perfumer, a large language model-based agentic framework that couples Quantum ESPRESSO with two predictive models. Across tested structures, pre-relaxation with Perfumer-relax model followed by QE refinement yielded a 2.75-fold overall speedup over QE alone. Perfumer-band model combines a periodic graph neural network with a latent Hermitian spectral head returns 12 band energies at any requested wavevector, preserving reciprocal lattice periodicity and time-reversal symmetry without constructing Hamiltonian. Trained on 125,153 self-curated band structures, Perfumer-band model reaches a median per-material mean absolute error of 0.157 eV on 2,607 test materials, including lanthanide, actinide and magnetic compounds, from held-out composition families spanning 85 elements, taking about 97 ms per material on two consumer CPU cores. The agent turns natural-language requests into relaxation-to-band workflows, from a single uploaded structure to automatically constructed new candidates and returns predicted properties.
